blocks.content: Where namespaces give a container its isolated view of the system, cgroups (control groups) are the Linux kernel feature that actually enforces how much of the host's real resources, CPU, memory, disk I/O, that container is allowed to use.

cgroups are organized around controllers, each responsible for limiting one resource type: the cpu controller caps processor time, memory caps RAM usage, blkio caps disk I/O, and pids caps how many processes a container can spawn, preventing a fork-bomb style attack.

blocks.alt: Different controllers, each governing a different resource

blocks.content: cgroups are organized in a tree, each container gets its own cgroup, nested under the system's overall resource hierarchy, letting the kernel enforce limits at exactly the granularity of an individual container, not just the host as a whole.

blocks.alt: Each container gets its own place in the hierarchy

blocks.content: 3. Where the Resource Limit Flags Actually Land
blocks.text: 3. Where the Resource Limit Flags Actually Land

blocks.content: This is the mechanism directly underneath the Resource Limits topic from the Docker Performance module, docker run --memory=512m is not some Docker-specific invention, it is simply Docker configuring the container's cgroup memory controller on your behalf.

blocks.alt: A familiar Docker flag, implemented as a cgroup setting

blocks.content: Older systems use cgroup v1, with separate, independent hierarchies per controller. Modern Linux distributions default to cgroup v2, a single, unified hierarchy covering every controller at once, simpler to reason about and what current Docker installations rely on by default.

blocks.alt: Modern systems have moved to one unified hierarchy

blocks.content: This ties directly back to the OOM-kill behavior covered in the Resource Limits topic, when a container exceeds its cgroup memory limit, it is the kernel's out-of-memory killer, acting on that specific cgroup, that terminates the offending process, not some separate Docker-level watchdog.

blocks.alt: The kernel itself enforces the limit, via the cgroup

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: cgroups are the kernel mechanism that actually enforces resource limits, organized into controllers (cpu, memory, blkio, pids) and a hierarchical structure.
Every --memory or --cpus flag on docker run is really just Docker configuring the corresponding cgroup controller on your behalf.
